transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-23
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE); Jordan Patel (Redwood SE); Ivy Rogers (Redwood CSM); Carlos Vega (CTO, Asterian); Priya Menon (Lead ML Eng); Samir Patel (Full-stack Eng); Lena Ortiz (Security)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick agenda — we do a short intro to the hosted API, then Jordan will demo streaming and params, we’ll cover retries and backoff, then peek at the Console Optimize suggestions. We’ll save Qs after each section.

[00:18] Carlos (Asterian): Thanks. high-level goal for us: we want chat responses under 200ms p50 and p95 under 600ms for simple retrieval-ish prompts. also we need to understand data controls — VPC or private options later.

[00:34] Maya: Got it. that latency target is tight but doable for short responses depending on model choice and batching. Jordan — show the simple streaming sample?

[00:48] Jordan (Redwood SE): Yeah, sure. I’ll share my screen — quick code sample in node. so we do a streaming chat request, you see partial tokens arrive as a chunk. this is the way applications render tokens as they come. in the SDK we default to a continuous stream. the payload here — messages array, model spec, and generation params like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop sequences.

[01:12] Samir (Asterian): Quick q — for interactivity, should we keep temperature at 0.0 for deterministic responses? or 0.2?

[01:21] Jordan: For UI chat where you want deterministic answers, 0 to 0.2 is typical. 0.0 is more deterministic but might be slightly repetitive. also note top_p interacts with temperature, so pick one to tune. we recommend starting with temp 0.1 and top_p 0.9 for most assistant flows.

[02:05] Jordan: Now on retries: the hosted API can surface transient errors — rate limit 429s or internal 5xx. our client libraries have an idempotency token option for generative calls so you can safely retry without duplicate side-effects. for non-idempotent calls we recommend an explicit dedupe layer.

[02:28] Lena (Security): when you say idempotency token, how are those stored? do you persist them in our side only or do you have retention? we need to track for audit logs SOC2.

[02:42] Maya: good q. logs and audit trails are available in Console — request ids, token-level cost and latency. for Private customers with VPC we can offer shorter retention windows and customer-managed KMS for encryption. we’ll share the security pack after the call.

[03:05] Priya: We do a lot of short prompts ~20 tokens, most are retrieval-augmented. how does batching interact with latency for small requests? we’re worried batching will increase tail latency.

[03:22] Jordan: Right — batching gives throughput gains but can add queuing delay. our runtime does dynamic batching where we bound batch wait time; you can configure target latency SLOs in the Dedicated plan. for Hosted, the default is conservative — it optimizes for low-latency for small requests, but for high QPS you’ll see batching kick in. in the Console Optimize tab we also show suggestions: enable prefix caching for repeated context, or configure KV-cache sizing.

[04:10] Carlos: KV cache — is that the same as the keys we store for repetition? i’ve seen docs call it K V cash which confused my team.

[04:18] Jordan: yeah sorry the docs sometimes are abbreviated — KV cache is token-level key-value cache used for decoder-only models to avoid recomputing earlier keys. helps when you have long histories and a lot of repeated prefixes.

[04:41] Samir: can you show us an example of a failed stream and how to recover on the client? we saw partial tokens then connection reset earlier in a POC.

[04:50] Jordan: Sure — demo time. I’ll start a stream and we’ll simulate a transient connection reset. when the socket drops, client should check the last accepted token index, then re-issue a request with an idempotency token and a partial context (or use the server-side KV cache if available). if you can’t resume, fall back to a fresh request but with a conservative backoff. the SDK includes automatic exponential backoff with jitter.

[05:35] Priya: you mentioned idempotency for generation — how do you prevent duplicated completions for say, a billing side-effect?

[05:44] Maya: For side-effects, the best practice is to separate generation from execution. generation is treated as a read; any write or billing action should be done after a deterministic confirmation step. we also support function/tool-calling patterns where the model returns structured JSON which you validate before executing.

[06:12] Carlos: in terms of models — which family should we pick for sub-second p95? our prompts are short but need good factuality.

[06:22] Jordan: Short prompts + high factuality, start with a medium-sized open model in the Redwood catalog tuned for low latency — we’ll recommend two candidates in the follow-up. if you need the absolute lowest latency we can point to smaller quantized variants or Dedicated with pinned capacity. tradeoffs: smaller model = lower cost and latency but may have lower factuality on complex queries.

[06:50] Samir: what about token billing for streaming partial tokens? do you get billed per partial chunk?

[06:57] Maya: Billing is per token emitted; partial chunks don’t change billing semantics. Console shows token counts and cost breakdown per request and per token.

[07:12] Jordan: switching to Console — I’ll flip to the Optimize tab. here you can upload representative prompts and get model suggestions, quantization recommendations, and caching hints. the Optimize tool will flag prompts with high-generation cost and show you where batching or caching can help.

[07:42] Jordan (screen): See this sample run: p50 120ms, p95 580ms on the medium model with 8ms kernel selection overhead. if we enable prefix caching and reduce max_tokens for these flows you can shave 30-40% from p95.

[08:05] Priya: does Optimize simulate our exact prompt distribution, or is it heuristic?

[08:12] Jordan: You can upload traces and Optimize will run against the selected model profile. it’s not a perfect playground but it gives actionable suggestions — like: reduce temperature for template responses, add a 0.2s target batch wait to increase throughput, or recommend quantized weights for Dedicated pools.

[08:45] Lena: Security wise — can we get SSO integration, RBAC, and customer-managed keys mentioned earlier? also audit logs retention policy?

[08:56] Ivy (CSM): Absolutely — we support SAML SSO, fine-grained RBAC in Console and for Private deployments you can bring your own KMS. retention windows can be configured per account for logs; default hosted retention is 90 days, and we have an enterprise add-on for extended retention.

[09:18] Carlos: timeline — we’re hoping to pilot next quarter. what’s a realistic path?

[09:25] Maya: Pilot: sandbox + benchmark this week, then a 2–4 week POC if results look good. if you need Dedicated or Private, that typically takes 4–8 weeks for provisioning and security review.

[09:40] Jordan: quick demo of a retry scenario in code — (reads) send request with idempotency-key, on 5xx do exponential backoff starting at 200ms doubling up to 3s with full jitter. on 429s backoff longer and respect Retry-After header. if you need guaranteed ordering/at-most-once semantics we can recommend a control-plane pattern.

[10:10] Samir: are there built-in client libraries for our stack — node/java/python?

[10:16] Maya: yes — official SDKs for node, python, and java. we also publish curl examples for quick smoke tests.

[10:31] Carlos: Ok, let's do the sandbox. we want the following in the invite: a) sample prompts, b) expected p95 targets, c) security checklist.

[10:39] Maya: noted. I will provision the sandbox and put those items in the ticket. Jordan will run a small latency script and record it. Ivy will attach security docs.

[10:52] Priya: one more technical question — for streaming token resume, do you recommend re-sending the full prompt history? that’s costly if the history is long.

[11:02] Jordan: If you have KV cache enabled, you can resume by sending just the delta and referencing the cache key — avoids re-sending entire history. otherwise you can hybird: send the recent window plus an identifier for the rest and rely on server-side cache where supported. still, if you often need resume, Dedicated gives better cache hit rates.

[11:30] Samir (interruption): lmk if you have a sample of the backoff code — i’ll try it after the call.

[11:34] Jordan: I'll paste the snippet in the ticket — small node example with idempotency and jitter.

[12:05] Maya: quick recap before Qs: 1) we demoed streaming and generation params; 2) discussed retries, idempotency tokens, and backoff; 3) Console Optimize can suggest batching/caching/quantization changes; 4) next steps: sandbox invite, benchmark run, security packet.

[12:28] Carlos: sounds good. two final asks: can we get a short checklist for when to pick Hosted vs Dedicated? and can you include estimated monthly cost for our projected QPS?

[12:40] Maya: yes — Jordan will draft a Hosted vs Dedicated decision checklist and we’ll include a cost estimate for your QPS scenarios.

[12:50] Ivy: I'll schedule the security follow-up with Lena for next week, and add the SOC2/KMS docs to the ticket.

[13:02] Maya: Great — thanks everyone. we’ll send the sandbox invite by EOD tomorrow and target the benchmark run mid-next week.

[13:12] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription quirks: occasional mis-attributions (Speaker 2 vs Jordan), some acronyms spelled out weirdly (K V cache / K V cash), slight stuttering in a few places, filler words retained.

References shared during call: sandbox invite link (sent later), Console Optimize sample screenshot (uploaded to ticket), security pack (link to docs).

End of transcript.
